name: PRP microneedling (vampire facial)

card.summary: Microneedling with a layer of your own platelet-rich plasma; popular and widely offered, but the added benefit of PRP is described as unproven, and unregulated spas have caused infections.
card.aka: Vampire facial; PRP facial; PRP microneedling
card.note: In 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections linked to an unlicensed spa offering vampire facials.

quick.overview:
PRP microneedling, marketed as the vampire facial, combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma prepared from the client's own blood. It is offered for skin texture, acne scars and general rejuvenation, and gained attention through celebrity endorsement in the 2010s.

Studies of microneedling are mostly small, and Wikipedia describes the efficacy of adding PRP as in question pending scientific studies. On looksmax.org, users post before-and-after accounts and discuss DIY variants such as PRP creams.
quick.mechanism: Blood is drawn and spun in a centrifuge to concentrate platelets, which carry growth factors, and the plasma is applied during or after microneedling, which makes tiny punctures in the skin. Proponents say the growth factors boost healing and collagen production.
quick.risks: The main concern raised in sources is infection when procedures are done in non-medical settings with poor infection control. In April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among patients of an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; about 200 other clients and partners tested negative. PRP is exempt from FDA regulation as a product, while the preparation devices need clearance.

lead: PRP microneedling, widely marketed as the vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure that combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), a concentrate of a person's own blood plasma that is rich in platelets. People use it to improve skin texture, acne scars and overall skin quality, and it is also discussed for under-eye and hair applications.[1][2]

PRP is made by centrifuging a blood sample to remove most red cells while retaining platelets, which carry growth factors and cytokines such as PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF and IGF-1; Wikipedia says the aim is to concentrate platelets to roughly three to five times normal levels.[1] Platelet concentrates differ in their preparation and are classified into several types in the literature.[3] Vampire facials grew popular in the 2010s with celebrity endorsement and social media attention, and usually involve microneedling.[1][11]

The evidence for PRP varies by use. Wikipedia describes the evidence as mixed as of 2020 across medical uses, and its microneedling article states that combining microneedling with PRP has efficacy in question pending scientific studies.[1][2] Safety attention rose in April 2024, when the CDC reported HIV diagnoses in clients of an unlicensed New Mexico spa that offered vampire facials.[1][2][14]
In looksmaxxing forums, members post before-and-after accounts, discuss PRP for acne scars, under-eyes and hair, and trade information about homemade PRP creams and at-home variants.[4][5][6][7][8]

paras: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, dermarolling or skin needling, involves repeatedly puncturing the skin with small sterile needles. Wikipedia distinguishes this cosmetic use from microneedling used for drug delivery or vaccination.[2] In the vampire facial, PRP prepared from the client's blood is applied to the skin around the needling, or injected into scars.[1][2] Preparation varies by person and facility.[1]

Platelet-rich plasma is also called autologous conditioned plasma. A blood sample is drawn and centrifuged, usually with a commercial kit, to remove most red blood cells and keep the platelets. Platelets can be activated with thrombin or calcium chloride, although this is not required.[1]

sections.h: Rationale and mechanism as described by proponents
paras: Platelets store growth factors and cytokines that are released in wound healing. Proponents say that placing a concentrate of them in skin that has just been needled supports healing and collagen remodelling, which they link to smoother texture and softened scars.[1] The needling itself creates controlled micro-injuries, and the collagen induction label reflects the idea that the skin's repair response builds new collagen.[2]

Researchers have noted that platelet concentrates are not all the same product. A 2009 classification distinguished pure platelet-rich plasma from leukocyte-rich preparations and platelet-rich fibrin, based on leukocyte content and fibrin architecture.[3] Wikipedia describes platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) as a development of PRP in which platelets and leukocytes sit in a fibrin matrix; it emphasises that the matrix influences the therapeutic effect, and its main documented uses are in oral and maxillofacial surgery.[12]
The procedure is offered for skin rejuvenation, fine lines, texture and acne scarring.[1][2] Wikipedia lists scarring and acne among the conditions microneedling has been used for.[2]

A 2021 paper in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology described a technique for performing PRP microneedling on a single hand, showing the combination has been adapted beyond the face.[10]

Wikipedia states that PRP has been studied for alopecia areata and androgenetic alopecia, possibly as an alternative to minoxidil or finasteride, and that interest in PRP for hair loss began around 2006.[1] The microneedling article reports that some studies combining microneedling with minoxidil found better hair outcomes than minoxidil alone.[2]

PRP is also used or studied in orthopaedics, wound care and assisted reproduction. Wikipedia summarises mixed results for tendon problems, tentative support for knee osteoarthritis, and a 2024 meta-analysis reporting benefits for venous and diabetic foot ulcers.[1]

Wikipedia states that the term platelet-rich plasma was first used in 1954 and that platelet blood banks appeared in the 1960s. PRP entered haematology in the 1970s and maxillofacial surgery about a decade later, and was used in an Italian cardiac surgery procedure in 1987.[1]

Interest in PRP for hair loss dates to about 2006.[1] The 2009 classification of platelet concentrates gave researchers a shared vocabulary for the different preparations.[3] In the 2010s, PRP attracted public attention through athletes and celebrities, and the vampire facial, usually a microneedling treatment with PRP, became a widely offered spa and clinic service.[1] In 2011 the World Anti-Doping Agency removed intramuscular PRP from its prohibited list, citing a lack of evidence of performance enhancement.[1]
A 2024 letter in Skin Research and Technology analysed Google Trends data to evaluate the effect of social media on the popularity of the vampire facial.[11]

Wikipedia reports mixed evidence for PRP across medical uses. A 2014 Cochrane review found very weak evidence of short-term pain reduction in tendon conditions, while 2019 and 2024 meta-analyses reported benefits in knee osteoarthritis and ulcers; PRP is reported to help hair loss conditions.[1]

For microneedling, Wikipedia describes the evidence as limited and mostly small studies, with some studies of microneedling plus minoxidil reporting better hair outcomes than minoxidil alone.[2] The same article says the efficacy of microneedling with PRP is in question pending scientific studies.[2] Published work specific to facial PRP microneedling includes technique papers and a classification of platelet concentrates rather than large controlled trials of appearance outcomes, though the dermatology literature includes many small split-face and comparison studies that are not summarised here.[3][10]

Wikipedia reports low adverse-effect rates for PRP in most trials, with weak evidence of harm.[1] The main risk it identifies for microneedling is infection when treatments are done in non-medical settings by untrained staff.[2]

In April 2024 the CDC reported that three women diagnosed with HIV had been patients at a spa in Albuquerque, New Mexico, after receiving vampire facials; about 200 other former clients and partners tested negative. Officials found the operator was unlicensed and had reused blood-contaminated single-patient equipment, and the New Mexico Department of Health warned that such treatments could spread blood-borne infections.[1][2][14][15] Wikipedia's dermal filler article also records the cluster.[13]

The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off label, while the devices used to prepare PRP require clearance.[1] Wikipedia also notes separate marketing of PRP for sexual function, which it says has no supporting evidence.[1]

Wikipedia credits celebrity endorsement for the 2010s popularity of the vampire facial.[1] The 2024 Google Trends letter examined how social media attention tracked public interest in the treatment.[11] Lemmy communities discussed the 2024 HIV reports under headlines such as 'CDC describes first known cases of HIV transmitted via vampire facial injections'.[14][15]

On looksmax.org, members post personal accounts of treatments. One poster describes PRP microneedling for acne scars left after steroid use, reporting that skin looked better the next day and that they planned further sessions, with one reply asking for a different guide.[4] Another member posted about drawing and processing their own blood for a first session, and replies joked about injecting one's own blood.[9] A third member described buying equipment for a clinic to offer vampire facials and PRF 'biofillers', the latter intended for areas such as tear troughs.[16]

Other threads discuss PRP for hair loss, with the original poster sharing a consumer health article,[5] and homemade PRP creams or serums intended to be applied after vampire facials, with the poster citing a study whose authors, in their words, had conflicts of interest.[6] Other thread titles show interest in at-home PRP, PRP for under-eyes and sourcing of PRP tubes.[7][8] Such posts are individual accounts and not controlled evidence.

Related practices include microneedling with other topicals, PRP injections for hair, platelet-rich fibrin and injectable biofillers, dermal fillers, and laser or radiofrequency resurfacing.[2][12][13][16]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, PRP is discussed both as a scar and skin treatment (vampire facial) and as a hair-loss option, with members sharing before-and-after posts and homemade variants [4][5][6].

claims.claim: PRP microneedling can clear acne scars within a few sessions
claims.believers: One member reports a visible improvement the day after a first session and expects acne scars to be fully removed after several treatments [4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes microneedling evidence as limited and mostly small studies, and says efficacy of adding PRP is in question pending scientific studies [2].

claims.claim: Applying PRP as a cream or serum after treatment improves absorption and results
claims.believers: A poster proposes making a PRP cream for daily use and after vampire facials to improve absorption and prevent dry plasma on the face, citing a published study [6].
claims.experts: No controlled studies of home-prepared topical PRP creams were loaded for this article; Wikipedia notes that PRP preparation varies by facility and that preparation devices require FDA clearance [1].

claims.claim: PRP is a worthwhile hair-loss treatment
claims.believers: A thread asks for opinions on PRP for hair loss, with the poster calling it promising and sharing a consumer health article [5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that PRP is described as helping alopecia areata and androgenetic alopecia, and says the evidence for PRP overall is mixed [1].

claims.claim: PRP can be done at home to save cost
claims.believers: Thread titles show members asking how to buy PRP tubes and whether home PRP is feasible [7][8].
claims.experts: The 2024 CDC-reported HIV cases involved an unlicensed spa reusing contaminated equipment, which Wikipedia cites as the infection risk of non-medical settings [1][2].

claims.claim: PRF 'biofillers' made from your own blood are a natural alternative to hyaluronic filler.
claims.believers: A member researching PRF filler products planned a regimen of monthly vampire facials alongside periodic PRF injections for under-eyes and other areas.[16]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes PRF mainly as an oral and maxillofacial surgery scaffold, with the strongest support in periodontal regeneration; it gives no outcome data for cosmetic facial use.[12]

claims.claim: The platelet growth factors are what make microneedling work better.
claims.believers: Proponents say platelet growth factors boost healing and collagen production when applied to needled skin.[1]
claims.experts: The microneedling article says efficacy of adding PRP remains in question pending scientific studies, and the platelet-concentrate literature shows that products differ in leukocyte and fibrin content.[2][3]

angle.goal: Skin texture, acne scars and overall skin quality
chain: Microneedling creates controlled micro-injuries in the skin
Platelet concentrate from the client's own blood is applied with it
Proponents say growth factors support healing and collagen, giving smoother, more even skin
angle.text: People book PRP microneedling to improve skin texture, post-acne scarring and a general fresher look. Microneedling is the physical treatment; PRP is the added layer that proponents say helps skin recover and rebuild collagen.
